title: Given a string, find the length of its longest palindromic subsequence, where a subsequence keeps relative order but need not be contiguous. Explain the Palindromic Subsequence DP pattern, the recurrence, the complexity, and a banking use case.
shortTitle: Longest Palindromic Subsequence (Longest Subsequence That Reads the Same Both Ways)
keyPoints: If the two ends of a range match, they both belong to the palindrome: add 2 to the answer for the inner range.
If the ends differ, drop one end and take the larger of the two shorter ranges.
A single character is a palindrome of length 1, which seeds the diagonal of the DP table.
Fill the table by increasing range length so every inner range is ready before the range that depends on it.
Time and space are both O(n^2) for the two-dimensional table.
This differs from the longest palindromic substring because gaps are allowed in a subsequence.

s1_definition.oneliner: Find the longest palindromic subsequence by comparing the two ends of each range: if they match add 2 to the inner answer, otherwise take the better of dropping either end.
s1_definition.profdef:
- **Range DP** – dp[i][j] is the length of the longest palindromic subsequence in the substring from index i to index j.
- **Match case** – when s[i] == s[j], those two characters wrap a palindrome: dp[i][j] = 2 + dp[i+1][j-1].
- **Mismatch case** – when s[i] != s[j], at least one end is not in the outer pair: dp[i][j] = max(dp[i+1][j], dp[i][j-1]).
- **Base case** – a single character is a palindrome of length 1: dp[i][i] = 1.
- **Fill order** – fill by increasing range length so inner ranges are ready before outer ranges.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India stores a reference code on each transaction and measures the longest symmetric core inside it. A symmetric core reads the same forward and backward when you are allowed to skip characters. The bank uses this as a lightweight integrity marker.

sections.s6_takeaway:
The Longest Palindromic Subsequence is the canonical Palindromic Subsequence DP problem, and the key insight is reasoning about a range by its two ends. If the characters at the left and right ends match, they form the outer layer of a palindrome, so the answer is 2 plus the longest palindromic subsequence of the inner range. If they differ, at least one end cannot be part of an outer pair, so you drop one end and take the larger of the two shorter ranges.

You build the table bottom-up, seeding the diagonal with 1 (every single character is a palindrome), then filling ranges of increasing length so that every inner range is ready before the outer range that depends on it. The answer sits in dp[0][n-1], the full range. The time and space are both O(n^2).

At the National Bank of India, Rajesh used this to measure the longest symmetric core inside each transaction reference code, because the bank used symmetric cores as lightweight integrity markers. The two-ended range DP over each code returned the length of the longest palindromic subsequence.

The senior-level insight is the LCS connection: the longest palindromic subsequence of a string equals the longest common subsequence of the string and its reverse. This alternative approach is equivalent in complexity but may be easier to implement when an LCS function is already available. Always clarify that the subsequence version allows gaps, which distinguishes it from the contiguous substring version.

Remember one sentence: match the ends and add 2 to the inner answer, or drop one end and take the larger, filling by increasing range length.
